Chemical engineering taught me to decompose complexity, reactors, flows, constraints into solvable systems. Case frameworks felt like an extension of that instinct, only applied to markets instead of mass balances. What drew me in was not the structure itself but the discipline it imposes: isolating drivers, quantifying trade-offs, and pressure-testing assumptions before committing to a recommendation. Working through profitability, market-entry, and operations cases sharpened how I think about ambiguity in industrial settings, where decisions rarely hinge on a single variable. My longer-term interest lies in strategy and consulting roles where engineering intuition meets commercial judgment diagnosing why a plant underperforms, why a category is losing margin, why an operating model needs rewiring. Frameworks, used well, are not templates; they are scaffolding for clear thinking under pressure.

Equity markets fascinate me because they are, at their core, a continuous referendum on how well capital is being deployed. Chemical engineering trained me to think in terms of inputs, conversion efficiency, and yield—an instinct that translates surprisingly well to evaluating businesses: margin structures, return on capital, and the quality of compounding. I have spent time dissecting annual reports, tracking commodity cycles, and modelling how operational choices ripple into valuation. What draws me to equity is the intellectual honesty it demands; theses are continuously tested by price. Long-term, I see myself in roles that connect industrial fundamentals with capital allocation - equity research, strategy, or principal investing, where engineering literacy and financial judgment together produce sharper, more defensible decisions.

Financial modelling appeals to me because it forces clarity, every assumption must be defensible, every driver traceable. Chemical engineering shaped this instinct early; balancing a reactor or sizing a unit operation is, in spirit, the same discipline as building a three-statement model: define the system, isolate variables, stress-test the boundaries. I have built operating models for listed companies, reverse-engineered valuations to understand what the market is implicitly pricing, and learned that the real rigour lies in sensitivities, not point estimates. Long-term, I see modelling as core infrastructure for the work I want to do—strategy, consulting, and capital allocation, where decisions involving plants, portfolios, or platforms must rest on numbers that survive scrutiny rather than narrative alone.

Criminology drew me in for a reason most would not expect of an engineer: it is fundamentally a study of systems failure. Crime patterns, deterrence, and recidivism are shaped by incentives, networks, and feedback loops - variables I have been trained to model in chemical engineering, where small parameter shifts cascade into very different outcomes. Reading into criminological theory sharpened how I think about behaviour, risk, and institutional design. That perspective matters commercially too: fraud analytics, compliance, financial crime, and corporate risk all sit at the intersection of human behaviour and quantitative inference. Long-term, I want to operate in strategy and analytics roles where understanding why systems fail is as valuable as knowing how to optimise them.

Music theory captivates me because it is, quite literally, mathematics you can hear. Intervals, harmonic progressions, and time signatures behave like governing equations—structured systems where small variations produce vastly different outcomes. Coming from chemical engineering, I found the parallels striking: both disciplines reward pattern recognition, proportion, and an instinct for when to follow rules and when to break them deliberately. Studying theory has sharpened how I listen, but also how I think, training me to hold structure and creativity in the same frame. That balance translates directly into the work I want to do in strategy and consulting, where the strongest decisions emerge from disciplined frameworks applied with judgment, taste, and a willingness to improvise.

This project develops Univision, an agentic computer vision system that replaces rigid pipelines with a dynamic, workflow-based architecture. At its core, a Central Orchestrator acts as a reasoning agent, autonomously selecting and sequencing specialized models—like YOLO for detection or CLIP for classification—based on the specific visual task at hand. By organizing these tools into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), the system efficiently passes data between nodes, performing complex multi-stage actions such as "detect, then crop, then analyze behavior." This agentic approach allows Univision to adapt its logic in real-time, focusing computational power only on relevant objects and providing a flexible, scalable framework for sophisticated visual reasoning.

This project explores the mathematical framework behind pricing financial derivatives, centered on the Black-Scholes-Merton model. You will begin by modeling asset price movements using Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM), incorporating stochastic calculus and Ito’s Lemma to account for market randomness. The core of the project involves deriving and solving the Black-Scholes partial differential equation (PDE) to determine the fair value of European options under the principle of no-arbitrage. Finally, you will implement numerical methods like Monte Carlo simulations and Binomial Trees to price complex "Exotic" options where analytical formulas don't exist, while calculating "The Greeks" (\Delta, \Gamma, \Theta) to manage and hedge market risk.

This project builds an automated trading system by first establishing a Data Pipeline to ingest market ticks and defining a Strategy Logic based on quantitative signals. You then validate the strategy through Backtesting, calculating risk-adjusted metrics like the Sharpe Ratio while ensuring the model isn't overfitted to historical data. Finally, you implement Risk Management protocols—including automated stop-losses and position sizing—and deploy the bot in a Paper Trading environment to verify performance under real-market latency before committing actual capital.

Every engineering system operates within an environment — and in real-world environments, decisions rarely exist in isolation. I am particularly drawn to applications beyond classical economics - in multi-agent systems, algorithmic game theory, and auction design. I also see Game Theory as a lens through which engineering decisions can be evaluated more honestly. A solution optimal in isolation may be suboptimal when other actors respond to it. Engineering trains you to understand how systems work. Economics trains you to understand why they behave the way they do. As an engineering student, I have spent years learning to optimize systems under well-defined constraints. Economics introduces me to a world where the constraints themselves are contested, where agents respond to incentives in ways that defeat naive optimization, and where equilibria emerge from the aggregate of countless individual decisions rather than from any central design. This shift in perspective is, to me, as intellectually significant as learning a new branch of mathematics.
I am particularly interested in the relationship between Economics and Game Theory — two subjects I am pursuing in parallel. Game Theory provides the formal scaffolding; Economics provides the empirical context. Together, they form a coherent framework for analyzing strategic behavior at every scale, from individual negotiation to market structure to policy design. Studying Economics will allow me to ground the abstract models of game-theoretic analysis in the real patterns of economic life.
Beyond its intellectual value, Economics is practically essential for anyone seeking to work at the intersection of technology, finance, and strategy. Understanding concepts such as incentive design, market failures, information asymmetries, and macroeconomic dynamics will make me a more perceptive analyst and a more effective decision-maker in any professional context I enter.

I grew up hearing news stories about crime the way most people do — as distant, dramatic headlines to be consumed and forgotten. It was not until I began asking why behind those headlines that something shifted. Why does crime cluster in certain neighbourhoods and not others? Why do some individuals who grow up in identical circumstances make radically different choices? Why do some societies imprison millions while others rehabilitate effectively with a fraction of the resources? These questions, I realised, do not have simple answers — and that is precisely what drew me in.
Criminology, as I understand it, is not simply the study of crime. It is the study of human behaviour at its most complex and consequential intersection — where psychology, sociology, economics, law, and politics all converge. What fascinates me is that it refuses easy narratives. The more seriously you engage with it, the more the comfortable explanations dissolve: crime is not simply a product of moral failure, nor purely of poverty, nor of broken systems alone. It emerges from a web of causes that criminology tries, rigorously and honestly, to untangle.
My interest deepened when I read about restorative justice practices in Scandinavian prison systems — the striking contrast with punitive models elsewhere, and the measurably different outcomes they produce. The gap between a model that can recall and one that can genuinely reason has always fascinated me. Reading through papers on RLHF and seeing how reward signals can steer a model toward coherent, multi-step thinking made me realize this isn't just an engineering trick — it's a fundamental question about how intelligence is shaped. I want to work on this project because I want to understand that shaping process from the inside: how you define a reward, how a policy learns to game or genuinely satisfy it, and where the whole framework breaks down. This feels less like a course and more like working on something that isn't fully solved yet.

I've used ML models enough to know when they work and not know why. That gap bothers me. I want to understand what actually guarantees generalization — not as a footnote in a textbook, but as something I can derive and reason about. Concentration inequalities and Rademacher complexity aren't just mathematical formalism to me; they're the honest answer to the question every ML practitioner quietly avoids. I'm drawn to this project because I want my intuition to be grounded in proof, not just pattern-matching from experience. If I'm going to work seriously in this field, I want the foundations to be real.

Human understanding has never been single-channel — we read body language while listening to words, we understand a news story differently when we see the image attached to it. I find it strange that for so long, ML systems were built to process one thing at a time. Multimodal learning feels like the field finally catching up to how perception actually works. I want to work on this because I'm curious about the alignment problem at the modality level — how do you build a shared representation space for things as different as a sentence and a video frame? That question sits right at the intersection of architecture design and theory, which is exactly where I want to be.

There's something uniquely satisfying about a model whose output you can see. I've spent enough time reading loss curves and accuracy metrics, and I want to work on something where the result is tangible — an image, a reconstruction, a transformation. But beyond the aesthetics, I'm drawn to generative models because they force you to think about what a model has actually learned about the world. A GAN that produces a convincing face has built some internal model of faces — and I want to understand what that model looks like, how it's structured, and how fragile it is. The progression from VAEs to StyleGANs in this project is exactly the kind of structured deep-dive I'm looking for.

Every abstraction I've ever used in ML — a CUDA kernel, a vectorized numpy operation, a batched forward pass — is hiding something. I want to stop hiding from it. I'm drawn to computer architecture because I think the best ML engineers eventually have to reckon with what's happening at the hardware level: why one implementation is ten times faster, why a certain memory access pattern destroys your cache, why branch misprediction matters when you're running inference at scale. This project appeals to me not because systems work is glamorous, but because I want the kind of understanding that doesn't have a ceiling — where knowing more always makes your higher-level work better.

My interest in finance did not begin in a classroom. It began at home, watching my father who has invested across equities, mutual funds, and bonds for as long as I can remember and has recently begun exploring venture capital. I observed him analyse capital structures, evaluate management quality, and think carefully about how companies finance their growth. I understood what he was doing directionally but I could never fully follow the underlying framework. That gap has stayed with me.
Over the past year at IIT Bombay I have actively pursued finance and strategy through multiple case competitions, the Winter Consulting programme at IIT Guwahati, and Quant 101 — the Finance Club's winter course, which gave me my first structured exposure to quantitative financial thinking. Building on that foundation I conducted a comprehensive investment analysis on Buyofuel — a Pre Series A biofuel marketplace, as part of my application to the Investment Team under the Finance Club, and completed a merger recommendation report on CRED and Smallcase analysing synergies, capital impact, and shareholder value creation.
These experiences were genuinely illuminating, but they also revealed a precise gap in my current capabilities. When building the Buyofuel investment thesis I could read and interpret financial statements but could not build my own projections from scratch. When justifying the CRED x Smallcase merger I could articulate why the combination created value strategically but lacked the formal valuation framework to quantify it rigorously. I was working with strong strategic intuition but without the full financial backing.
Corporate Finance is exactly that. Two months of structured mentored learning in valuation methodologies, capital structure theory, and financial decision making frameworks would directly address the gap I have identified in my own work. My goal is not to add another credential to a list. It is to reach a point where I can walk into any finance or consulting room and speak this language with genuine depth, build a financial model from first principles, and formally value a company the way a professional analyst would.

My engagement with finance over the past year has been intensive but deliberately focused. Through the Winter Consulting programme at IIT Guwahati, Quant 101 conducted by the Finance Club, multiple case competitions spanning domains from renewable energy to consumer strategy, and a comprehensive investment analysis conducted as part of my application to the Investment Team under the Finance Club, I have developed a working understanding of how capital flows into early stage businesses, how investment theses are built, and how financial decisions are evaluated at the company level.
But the more deeply I have engaged with these questions the more I have become aware of how much of the broader investment landscape I am still not seeing. I understand how venture capital works — how deals are structured, how startups are evaluated, and how returns are generated over a long investment horizon. But I do not yet understand how VC fits within the portfolio of a large institutional investor like a pension fund or university endowment — why they allocate to an asset class that is illiquid, high risk, and takes a decade to return capital alongside more stable alternatives. I understand that private equity, hedge funds, real assets, and private credit all exist alongside VC as investment categories but I do not yet understand how they interact with each other, why sophisticated investors choose one over another at different points in a market cycle, and how each generates returns through structurally different mechanisms.
Every time I evaluated a startup or analysed a merger I was making decisions within a narrow frame, without fully understanding the larger ecosystem of capital allocation that those decisions exist within.
Alternative Investments is the subject that addresses this gap directly. Two months of structured mentored exploration of how different asset classes behave, how institutional portfolios are constructed across VC, PE, hedge funds, and real assets, and how the alternative investment landscape in India is evolving would give me the broader conceptual map that my intensive but focused financial experience has been missing.

Some of my earliest memories of finance are sitting with my father as he made carefully considered decisions about which companies deserved his capital. He has been investing in equities for as long as I can remember and watching him do it with such deliberateness and conviction always fascinated me. But fascination and understanding are different things. I could see what he was doing. I could not yet do it myself.
Over the past year at IIT Bombay I have been building my financial foundation from a different direction. Through Quant 101 conducted by the Finance Club, the Winter Consulting programme at IIT Guwahati, multiple case competitions, and a comprehensive investment analysis on a Pre Series A company as part of my Investment Team application, I have developed a working understanding of how early stage private companies are evaluated- how investment theses are built, how deal structures work, and how capital flows into businesses before they reach public markets.
I do not yet formally understand how a company is valued. I understand how a VC analyst thinks about a business. I do not yet understand how an equity research analyst thinks about the same business from the public market side, how they read financial statements, how they arrive at a target price, and how macro factors, sentiment, and fundamentals interact to determine what a stock is actually worth.
This contrast- between private market thinking which I have been building and public market thinking which I have not yet formally developed, is precisely what draws me to Finance Equity. My father's process, which I observed for years without fully understanding, is rooted in exactly this discipline. Two months of structured mentored learning in equity analysis, stock valuation methodology, and financial statement interpretation would give me the formal framework to finally understand what I have been watching all along and to develop my own independent analytical capability in public markets alongside the private market foundation I have already been building.
I am applying not because equity is new to me as a concept — it has been part of my household for as long as I can remember. I am applying because I am finally ready to move from observer to analyst.

My father has never invested in just one thing. For as long as I can remember he has maintained a portfolio that spans equities, mutual funds, bonds, and more recently venture capital, each allocation deliberate, each serving a different purpose within a larger financial picture. As a child I understood individual investments in isolation- this stock, that fund, this bond. What I never fully understood was the logic that connected them. Why these proportions. Why this balance between risk and return. Why shift allocations as circumstances change. The portfolio as a whole always felt like something more than the sum of its parts and I could never quite see what that something was.
Over the past year at IIT Bombay I have been systematically building my financial knowledge from the ground up. Through Quant 101 conducted by the Finance Club, the Winter Consulting programme at IIT Guwahati, multiple case competitions, a comprehensive Pre Series A investment analysis, and a merger recommendation report, I have developed working knowledge across several distinct domains of finance. I do not yet have the framework that shows me how the pieces fit together.
Applied Portfolio Management is precisely that framework. It is the subject that sits above individual investment decisions and asks the harder question- given everything you know about individual assets, how to construct a coherent collection of them that deliberately balances risk and return, adapts to changing market conditions, and serves a clear investment objective. How you move from picking individual winners to managing a portfolio that performs as a whole. How professional fund managers think differently from individual analysts and what that shift in perspective requires.
Two months of structured mentored learning in portfolio construction, risk management, and applied investment strategy would give me the synthesis I have been building toward, the framework that finally connects everything I have been learning into a coherent and actionable whole.
I am applying because I have spent a year learning the individual pieces. I am ready to understand how they fit together.

Stochastic processes are the load-bearing mathematics of quantitative finance, and I want to encounter them properly with the time to build intuition rather than under the time pressure of a semester. I will be taking the course in my upcoming semester, and rather than wait to meet Markov chains, martingales, and Brownian motion only inside an exam-driven framework, I want to spend the summer engaging with them in the way they reward most: slowly, with attention to the structural ideas behind the computations.
My motivation comes from work I have already done at the surface of these objects without the formal grounding they deserve. At the IIT Bombay Winter Quant Challenge I ranked 6th out of 224 on problem sets built around Markov chains and expected value, and through the Winter School of Quantitative Finance I worked on forward and option pricing, Greeks, and a NIFTY 50 backtesting exercise with 99% VaR. A personal project building a FinBERT-based sentiment pipeline for GOOGL price prediction made me increasingly aware that I was modelling stochastic phenomena with ad hoc tools. Concretely, I would like to spend the summer working through (i) discrete-time martingales and Markov chain theory from a rigorous standpoint, (ii) the measure-theoretic foundations needed to handle Brownian motion and continuous-time martingales properly, and (iii) Itô's lemma and the Black-Scholes PDE derivation from first principles. Combinatorial game theory is, I think, one of the genuinely beautiful corners of mathematics — and one whose accessibility belies its depth. The path from Nim to Sprague-Grundy values to surreal numbers is the kind of mathematical journey I have wanted to take since first reading about Conway's construction. My olympiad background — two appearances at RMO and the Maharashtra-level selection — gave me a taste for problems where the right definition is half the battle, and CGT seems to live almost entirely in that territory.
What draws me to this project specifically is the balance between theoretical depth and concrete computability. I would like to work through the foundational theory of impartial and partizan games (Sprague-Grundy, the construction of games as {L | R}, the embedding of surreal numbers and ordinals), and then push into temperature theory and thermographs, where the analysis of "hot" games starts to feel less like recreational mathematics and more like real structural theory.
My competitive experience also informs this interest in a less obvious way. Building strategies for Citadel Terminal and IMC Prosperity taught me that adversarial reasoning benefits enormously from the right abstraction — knowing what a position "is worth" matters more than knowing what moves are available from it. CGT formalizes this intuition. Concretely, over the summer I would like to (i) work through Sprague-Grundy and the surreal number construction up to the embedding of the reals, (ii) analyze a partizan game such as Domineering on small boards using temperature theory, and (iii) write up the proofs carefully — theory projects without a written artifact rarely stick.

Particle Physics has long been the most fascinating aspect of Quantum Mechanics for me as an EP student. Concepts such as Paul Dirac’s prediction of antiparticles, particle–antiparticle annihilation, the structure of the Standard Model, and the discovery of the Higgs Boson have always sparked my curiosity However, my exposure to these topics has mostly been through scattered discussions and popular-level explanations, leaving me with an intuitive but unstructured understanding of the field.
Through this summer project, I hope to develop a more rigorous and coherent understanding of particle physics by connecting these ideas to the formal framework of quantum theory as given in Griffiths.

Relativity initially seemed highly unintuitive to me, but my perspective changed significantly after taking PH110. I was fascinated by how a few simple postulates of Special Relativity could lead to such profound and counterintuitive consequences. Concepts such as the geometry of Minkowski Spacetime, Lorentz Transformation, simultaneity, and time dilation particularly captured my interest because they fundamentally reshape our intuitive understanding of space and time.
My exposure to General Relativity, however, has so far been limited to a qualitative understanding — primarily the idea that gravity arises from the curvature of spacetime. The mathematical framework behind the theory, especially topics such as differential geometry, tensors, and manifolds, seems both challenging and intellectually exciting, and I am eager to understand how these mathematical structures describe physical reality.
Since relativity is not a core component of the EP curriculum, this project presents a valuable opportunity for me to build a systematic foundation in the subject. I believe this project will provide an important base for exploring advanced topics in astrophysics, cosmology, and theoretical physics in the future.

Ever since our EP DIC PH109 course introduced me to Statistical Mechanics, I have been eager to study the subject more formally. What initially attracted me to the field was the realization that macroscopic physical laws can emerge naturally from the collective behavior of an enormous number of microscopic constituents. I found it especially fascinating that phenomena as fundamental as the direction of heat flow or the approach to thermal equilibrium have deep statistical origins rooted in ideas such as probability distributions, the Central Limit Theorem, and the Law of Large Numbers.

As I explored the subject further, I learned how broadly statistical mechanics applies across physics, from thermodynamics and kinetic theory to modern areas such as Condensed Matter Physics and phase transitions. 

While I believe I have developed a reasonable understanding of the basic principles of the subject, my knowledge is still largely introductory. Through this project, I hope to build a more rigorous and mathematical understanding of statistical mechanics, especially the connections between microscopic dynamics, probability, and macroscopic observables.

Topology and Group Theory are two areas of mathematics that I recently discovered and became very eager to explore further. What initially drew me toward these subjects was their seemingly abstract nature — ideas involving manifolds, symmetries, and transformations felt mathematically elegant 
Although my understanding of these topics is still quite limited, I have become increasingly interested in concepts such as Abelian groups, Lie Groups, and their applications in modern physics. In particular, learning about the connection between symmetry principles and conservation laws through Noether's Theorem made me realize how deeply mathematics and theoretical physics are intertwined.

Through this project, I hope to gain a more systematic and rigorous introduction to these subjects and develop the mathematical maturity needed to approach advanced areas of theoretical physics. More importantly, I hope this experience will provide both the guidance and motivation to continue exploring these relatively unfamiliar but highly intriguing areas of mathematics and physics in greater depth.

What does a Russian mathematical feud, the hydrogen bomb, and Google's billion-dollar algorithm have in common? A single, elegant idea: the Markov Chain.

It started with a Veritasium video. What I expected to be a casual watch turned into one of those rare moments where mathematics suddenly feels *alive*. The story begins not with a breakthrough, but with an argument. In the early 20th century, the Law of Large Numbers — the bedrock of probability — was believed to apply only to *independent* events. A Russian theologian and mathematician, Nekrasov, even used this to argue that free will existed, since human choices were "dependent" and therefore beyond the reach of probability. Andrey Markov found this infuriating. So he set out to prove that probability theory could govern dependent events too — and in doing so, accidentally invented one of the most powerful mathematical tools in history.

The chain is disarmingly simple: the future depends only on the present, not the past. Yet this memoryless elegance unlocked doors no one anticipated. Decades later, Stanislaw Ulam, stuck in bed recovering from illness and playing solitaire, wondered if he could use random sampling to estimate probabilities too complex to calculate directly. This idea — the Monte Carlo method — was built on Markovian thinking, and it went on to model neutron behavior in nuclear fission, becoming a cornerstone of the Manhattan Project and the development of the first thermonuclear bomb. A card game, a sick mathematician, and Markov chains quietly shaped the atomic age.

Then came the internet. Early search engines drowned in irrelevance — they ranked pages by keywords, not quality. Google changed everything with PageRank, which modeled the web as a Markov Chain: imagine a random surfer clicking links endlessly, and the pages they land on most often are the most important. That probabilistic insight — pure Markov — built the world's most powerful search engine.

From a petty academic dispute to nuclear physics to the algorithm that indexes human knowledge: I want to understand this thread. This project is my chance to go beyond the awe of the Veritasium video and get my hands into the actual mathematics — the transition matrices, the stationary distributions, the convergence theorems — and see for myself why something so simple predicts almost anything.

The idea that a system can be completely deterministic and yet utterly unpredictable feels almost contradictory. No randomness, no missing information — just equations, playing out — and still, you cannot know where they lead. That tension is what pulled me in. It made me question how much of what I'd learned about "solving" systems was just a comfortable simplification of a far messier, far more interesting reality.
Non-linear dynamical systems are that reality. And I want to study them not because they're famously difficult, but because the chaos they produce isn't truly chaos — there's geometry in it, structure in it, and I want to find it.
This project is my first real step into that world, and I can't think of anything I'd rather be doing this summer.

Everything I learned in physics made sense. Push something, it moves. Look at something, it's there. Cause and effect, clean and simple.
Then I encountered quantum mechanics, and everything I thought I knew quietly fell apart.
At the quantum scale, a particle doesn't have a fixed position until you actually look at it — and the act of looking is what forces it to decide. Two particles, separated by vast distances, can somehow still "know" what the other is doing instantly. Things pass through walls they have no business passing through. The universe at its smallest scale behaves nothing like the universe we see and touch every day — and the strangest part is, nobody fully understands why. Not even the physicists who work with it daily.
I want to spend this summer digging into that gap — between what the equations say and what the human mind can actually imagine — and see how far I can get.

I grew up on a mountain slope where aeroplanes were rare visitors to the sky. As a child, I would lie flat on a rock and watch the occasional aircraft trace a thin line overhead, completely mystified by the fact that something so large could stay up there at all. Around the same time, I watched a film in which an air force officer built his own aeroplane from scratch, and from that point on, the idea that an ordinary person could understand flight well enough to actually build a flying machine took root in me. That childhood ambition has matured over the years, but it has never really left.
Today, I am a first-year M.Tech. student at IIT Bombay, specialising in Systems and Controls. Most of my work so far has been on quadcopters, self-balancing robots, and embedded systems, which has given me a solid foundation in the control and electronics side of flying machines. I am comfortable with calculus, differential equations, Python, and MATLAB, and I have learned to think about dynamic systems in terms of state, feedback, and stability. What I have slowly come to realise, though, is that the control side is only half of the picture. A controller can only do as much as the underlying physics permits, and when the system in question is an aircraft, that underlying physics is aerodynamics.
This gap became very real for me during the RC Plane competition organised by the Aeromodelling Club at IIT Bombay, where my team built and successfully flew an RC aircraft. Working on that project was both exhilarating and humbling. We managed to get the plane in the air, but I was very aware that many of our design choices, like airfoil selection, wing sizing, and control surface placement, were guided more by convention and intuition than by any real first-principles understanding. I could model the dynamics of the aircraft as a control system, but I could not yet derive the aerodynamic coefficients that fed into that model. I want to close that gap.
This is exactly why this project draws me. Building up from continuity and Bernoulli's equation through viscosity, boundary layers, and the laminar-to-turbulent transition is precisely the foundation I am missing, and topics like flow separation and drag directly shape the plant model any controller has to work with. My goals are fairly concrete. I want to develop a rigorous physical understanding of incompressible and viscous flow instead of treating aerodynamic forces as black-box coefficients. I want to build the analytical toolkit that will let me make informed design decisions on my own. And I want to apply what I learn to a focused problem, ideally an airfoil or wing section relevant to the small UAVs and RC aircraft I already work with. More broadly, I see this project as the bridge between my current control-systems expertise and the integrated aerospace work I hope to pursue, from autonomous UAVs to the more ambitious flying machines that have fascinated me since those days on the rock. I am committed to giving it the time, rigour, and curiosity it deserves.

Like a lot of children of my generation, my first real encounter with genetics came from Jurassic Park. The idea that a strand of DNA preserved in amber could be coaxed back into a living, breathing creature was thrilling, and even after I grew old enough to understand that the science was more fiction than fact, the underlying premise stayed with me. If life really is written in a four-letter code, then learning to read that code, and eventually to write in it, felt like one of the most extraordinary things a person could do. That fascination shaped a small but meaningful turn in my schooling. When I had to choose my stream in Class 11, I picked biology specifically because I wanted to understand what was actually going on inside that code.
Those two years gave me my first proper introduction to the subject. I learned the basics of DNA and inheritance, and I still remember the simple lab where we extracted DNA from green peas using nothing more than detergent, salt, and alcohol, watching that pale, stringy thread settle out of the solution. It was a small experiment, but seeing something so abstract become physically visible left an impression that has never quite faded. Around the same time, I worked through Mendel's pea-plant crossings and tried to wrap my head around the genetics of blood groups, where the neat dominant-recessive picture I had just learned suddenly became more complicated with co-dominance and multiple alleles. That was the first time I really understood that genetics was not just a set of clean rules to memorise, but a living puzzle with exceptions and surprises everywhere you looked.
After Class 12, my academic path took me towards engineering, and I am currently a first-year M.Tech. student at IIT Bombay specialising in Systems and Controls. I have not formally studied biology since, but my curiosity about genetics has never really gone away.
Honestly, my reason for wanting to take this project is simple. I want to learn more about the subject for its own sake. I am not coming into this with a grand plan or a career pivot in mind. I am coming into it as someone who has been quietly curious about genetics for more than a decade and finally has the chance to sit down and properly satisfy that curiosity. That, more than anything else, is what draws me to this project.

My interest in the brain started with a television show. Brain Games was the kind of programme that took something I had always taken completely for granted, my own perception of the world, and quietly demolished it episode after episode. Optical illusions that my eyes refused to see correctly even when I knew the trick, memory experiments that showed how unreliable my own recollections were, attention demonstrations where I missed things happening in plain sight. Every episode left me with the same uncomfortable, exciting thought: the version of reality I was experiencing was not really out there but was being constructed somewhere inside my head, and I had almost no idea how. That curiosity has stayed with me ever since.
The interest became more personal when my grandfather developed Parkinson's disease. Watching someone I loved slowly lose control over his own movements, while the person inside remained, was a difficult and clarifying experience. It made the brain stop being an abstract puzzle for me. Behind every clinical description of a neurological disease is a family watching it happen, and somewhere in the structure of those neural circuits is the difference between a person being themselves and a person being taken from us in pieces. I do not pretend that taking one project on neuroscience will let me do anything about that, but I would at least like to understand, properly, what was happening to him.
I am currently a first-year M.Tech. student at IIT Bombay specialising in Systems and Controls, with a background in embedded systems, robotics, and signal processing. The brain, in many ways, is the most extraordinary control system any of us will ever encounter, and I find myself returning again and again to the same set of questions about it. How does this roughly one-and-a-half kilogram organ process the staggering amount of visual, auditory, and sensory information flowing into it every second, and somehow stitch it all into a single coherent experience? Where, in all of that activity, does the thing we call consciousness actually live? There is something quietly funny about the fact that I am sitting here using my brain to write an application about learning how the brain works, and that recursive strangeness is itself part of what fascinates me.
The list of things I want to understand keeps growing. I am curious about brain-computer interfaces and the idea that one day we may genuinely be able to control machines with thought alone, which feels like science fiction and active research at the same time. I am curious about dreams, about why the brain spends hours every night generating entire imaginary worlds for an audience of one. I am curious about déjà vu, that small uncanny moment when the brain seems to glitch and convinces you that the present has already happened. Each of these is a small window into a much larger question about how the most familiar thing in the world, our own minds, is also the most mysterious.
My reason for wanting to take this project is straightforward. I want to learn how the brain actually works, at the level of neurons, circuits, and the larger systems they build into. I want to understand, even at a beginner's level, what diseases like Parkinson's and Alzheimer's are really doing to those circuits. And I want to give the curiosity that started with a television show and was sharpened by my grandfather's illness the structured, sustained attention it has deserved for a long time.

My first real exposure to quantum mechanics came, slightly embarrassingly, from The Big Bang Theory. I started watching it as a teenager, and although the show was a sitcom first and a physics lesson somewhere far down the list, the constant background hum of references to Schrödinger's cat, wave-particle duality, string theory, and the strange behaviour of very small things planted a question in my head that I could not quite shake. The characters spoke about quantum mechanics with the easy familiarity of people who had grown up inside it, and I remember thinking that whatever this subject actually was, I wanted to one day be able to follow that conversation properly rather than just laughing at the jokes.
The Class 11 and 12 physics textbook gave me my first proper, if very gentle, introduction. I read about Schrödinger's cat as a thought experiment, met the Schrödinger equation in its simplest form, and was introduced to the uncertainty principle, spin, and angular momentum, mostly as ideas rather than as a working mathematical framework. Even at that surface level, it was clear that quantum mechanics was unlike anything else I had studied. Classical physics had always felt intuitive in the end, even when it was difficult. Quantum mechanics felt like the rules of the universe quietly changing once you looked closely enough, and I have wanted to look more closely ever since.
I am currently a first-year M.Tech. student at IIT Bombay specialising in Systems and Controls. My background is in classical control systems, embedded electronics, and robotics, but my interest in quantum has been kept alive at IIT Bombay in a very direct way. A senior of mine here is doing his PhD research in quantum control, and watching him work has made me realise that quantum mechanics is not just a beautiful piece of physics from a hundred years ago, but a living, active field where the mathematics I have spent years building comfort with, linear algebra, differential equations, operators, state-space thinking, actually shows up in central ways. That overlap with my own training is part of what makes this the right moment for me to finally take quantum mechanics seriously.
I am also genuinely fascinated by quantum computing, and the idea that the strange features of the quantum world, superposition, entanglement, measurement, can be turned into a new form of computation feels like one of the most exciting frontiers of the next few decades. Somewhere down the line, I would like to explore quantum control theory more deeply, possibly as a research direction of my own. But I am very aware that any of that has to rest on a real, foundational understanding of quantum mechanics first, and that is exactly what this project offers. Working through the postulates, the wavefunction and its interpretation, the Schrödinger equation, Hilbert spaces, operators, uncertainty, spin and angular momentum, and the role of symmetries with texts like Griffiths and Shankar is the foundation I need, taught the way it deserves to be taught.
My reason for wanting to take this project is therefore both honest and concrete. I want to finally understand quantum mechanics properly, in its own language, rather than through analogies and sitcom one-liners. I want to build the foundation that would let me eventually engage seriously with quantum computing and quantum control, fields I am increasingly drawn to. And more than anything, I want to give a curiosity that has been with me since my teenage years the structured, mathematically serious attention it has been quietly waiting for.

My first year at IITB genuinely changed how I think about physics. In CH117, quantum mechanics fascinated me — particularly how the Schrödinger equation, a differential equation, could encode something as fundamental as the probabilistic nature of reality. In MA110, I developed a strong foundation in the mathematical tools — differential equations, linear algebra — that I now understand underlie most of modern physics.
Special and General Relativity feels like the natural next step. I've become increasingly interested in particle physics and high energy physics as a long term direction, and I understand that Special Relativity is not optional for that path — everything at accelerators like CERN operates in relativistic regimes. The combination of QM and Special Relativity is what gives rise to Quantum Field Theory, which I want to eventually understand. I need to build that foundation properly, and this project is where that starts.
Beyond the practical, the content itself draws me in — spacetime, time dilation, curved geometry, black holes, Einstein field equations. These are ideas I want to understand rigorously, not just intuitively.
I have no formal prerequisites beyond MA110 and CH117, but I believe that mathematical maturity and genuine curiosity are what this project actually requires.

I come as someone who has built a genuine foundation and is hungry to go further to engage rigorously with the material, ask harder questions, and enrich my understanding in ways that self-study alone cannot provide.

Of all the areas of mathematics I have encountered so far, probability feels the most alive. It is the language in which uncertainty speaks, and once you start seeing the world through it, you cannot stop. The way a random walk describes Brownian motion, the way Markov chains model systems with no memory of the past beyond the present state, the way stochastic processes underpin everything from signal processing to financial derivatives . it is one of those topics where the deeper you go, the more connected everything becomes.
I am a first year student in the EEDD at IIT Bombay. Probability and random processes is not just a course I am required to take, it is genuinely one of my favourite areas of mathematics. There is something deeply satisfying about the rigour of it: the way measure theoretic ideas give a solid foundation to intuitions we often take for granted, the way the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem emerge from first principles, and the way conditional expectation becomes a tool of remarkable power once you understand it properly.
My interest in this topic is not purely theoretical. I am actively working toward a career in quantitative finance, and random processes sit at the absolute heart of that field. I have been independently building a stock market prediction model using LSTM networks, working with historical price data to model temporal dependencies in financial time series. That work pushed me to understand concepts like stationarity, autocorrelation, and the difficulty of modelling non stationary stochastic sequences in a principled way. It made me realise how much of what quantitative researchers do every day is applied probability: pricing derivatives through risk neutral measures, modelling volatility as a stochastic process, detecting regime changes using hidden Markov models. To do any of that well, you need a deep and honest understanding of the foundations.
This is exactly what I am hoping to build through this project. I want to go beyond surface level familiarity and develop the kind of rigorous intuition for random processes that will make me a stronger researcher and eventually a stronger quant. I want to work through the mathematics carefully, understand where the standard results come from, and start seeing how they connect to real problems in engineering and finance.
I come with genuine enthusiasm for the subject, an ongoing project that already sits at the intersection of probability and machine learning, and a clear long term direction that makes this foundation matter. I am not taking this project to fill a summer. I am taking it because it is exactly what I need to learn next.
